title: The council of the gods
greek: conciliumque vocat divum pater atque hominum rex
short: Book X opens, like Iliad VIII, with Jupiter summoning the gods; the debate between Venus and Juno ends with Jupiter declaring himself neutral.
body: The only full divine assembly in the Aeneid. Its model is Homer's councils on Olympus, above all Iliad 8.1-27, where Zeus forbids the gods to help either side, and Iliad 4.1-72. Conington and Nettleship note that the opening line probably marks a new day, since Homer's councils meet at dawn, and that Virgil pictures the gods' palace as a great Roman temple with doors at both ends ('tectis bipatentibus', 10.5); when the gods escort Jupiter to the door at the end (10.116-17) Conington suggests Virgil is thinking of a Roman consul escorted from the senate. The scene is built as a debate in the Roman manner: Venus pleads (10.18-62), Juno replies point by point (10.63-95), and Jupiter gives judgement (10.104-13). Conington's introduction to the book is sharp about the result: Jupiter's ruling is 'a conclusion in which nothing is concluded', since he will let events run as fate decides. Modern readers have seen in this neutrality a deliberate statement of the relation between Jupiter and fate (see the note on 'Jupiter is one and king over all').

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 234, note on 10.1 and 10.5, and introduction to Book 10
S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.1-117

title: Carthage and the Alps (Hannibal)
greek: cum fera Karthago Romanis arcibus olim / exitium magnum atque Alpis immittet apertas
short: Jupiter looks forward to Hannibal's invasion of Italy in 218 BC: that, not the present war, will be the proper time for hatred.
body: Jupiter tells the gods that the 'due time of battle' (iustum pugnae tempus) will come when Carthage 'shall open the Alps' and bring 'great ruin' on Rome's citadels: Hannibal's crossing of the Alps and the Second Punic War (218-201 BC). The prophecy reaches back to Dido's curse in Book IV, where she prays for an avenger to rise from her bones (4.625-9). Servius notes the force of the phrase: Virgil does not say Hannibal sent an army through the Alps, but that he broke open the Alps themselves, which Cato and Livy had called Italy's wall. Conington and Nettleship treat 'Alpes apertas' as almost a hendiadys with 'exitium magnum' (the destruction comes through the opened Alps). They also explain the next line, 'tum res rapuisse licebit' (then they may plunder), as an old Roman legal phrase for open war, after the fetial demand for satisfaction had been refused (Servius discusses the ceremony of clarigatio here). Livy narrates the crossing at 21.32-38.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 236, note on 10.13
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.13

anchor: my wounds are yet to come
title: Venus wounded by Diomedes
greek: equidem credo, mea vulnera restant
short: Venus bitterly recalls Iliad V, where Diomedes, son of Tydeus, wounded her hand as she carried Aeneas from battle.
body: Venus fears that 'a second son of Tydeus' will rise against Troy from Arpi in Apulia, where Diomedes now rules (the Latins sent envoys to him in 8.9-17; his refusal is reported in 11.243-95). Her sarcastic 'I believe my wounds are still to come' points to Iliad 5.330-43, where Diomedes pursued Aphrodite as she rescued Aeneas and cut her wrist with his spear, so that she dropped her son and fled to Olympus. Conington and Nettleship stress the emphatic 'mea': 'my wounding, too, is not yet done with', and gloss 'restant' as 'remain to be completed'. The detail is typical of Venus' speech, which piles up grievances, many of them exaggerated, to move Jupiter. The irony is that in Book XI Diomedes himself recalls this wound as the sacrilege that cost him his homecoming, and refuses to fight Aeneas again.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 237, note on 10.29

title: Amathus, Paphos, Cythera, Idalium
greek: est Amathus, est celsa mihi Paphus atque Cythera / Idaliaeque domus
short: Venus lists her own cult-centres, two of them on Cyprus, as a quiet refuge where Ascanius could live without glory.
body: Amathus, Paphos and Idalium are towns on Cyprus, the island most closely bound to Aphrodite's worship; Cythera is the island off the south of the Peloponnese. Hesiod's Theogony (188-200) tells how the goddess, born from the foam, came first to Cythera and then to Cyprus, which explains her titles Cytherea and Cypris. Conington and Nettleship cite Herodotus 5.104 for Amathus and Tacitus, Annals 3.62, for its temple of Venus; Herodotus 1.105 reports the shrine on Cythera. Venus is pretending to give up the destiny of Rome: let Ascanius live 'inglorious' (inglorius) in one of her sanctuaries. Juno answers with the same list thrown back in her face ('Paphos is thine and Idalium, thine high Cythera', 10.86): if those are Venus' places, why meddle in Italy?

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 239, note on 10.51

title: The 'adulterous Dardanian' (Paris)
greek: me duce Dardanius Spartam expugnavit adulter
short: Juno names Paris only by insult, and turns his abduction of Helen into an armed assault on Sparta, so that the fall of Troy becomes just revenge.
body: Juno's speech answers Venus by blaming the Trojans for everything. Paris, a descendant of Dardanus, is 'the Dardanian adulterer' who 'stormed Sparta' (expugnavit). Conington and Nettleship take the verb literally: Juno exaggerates, presenting Paris' voyage as an invasion that sacked Sparta, so that the sack of Troy looks like fair retribution; they compare Hector's rebuke of Paris at Iliad 3.46-51, where he sails with comrades across the sea and carries off a woman from a far land. Juno also hints at Venus' own guilt: 'did I send the shafts of passion?', since Venus gave Helen to Paris as his prize for judging her the most beautiful. That judgement of Paris is one of the causes of Juno's anger named at the very start of the poem (1.27, 'spretae iniuria formae').

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 244, note on 10.92

title: 'Rex Iuppiter omnibus idem': Jupiter and fate
greek: sua cuique exorsa laborem / fortunamque ferent. rex Iuppiter omnibus idem. / fata viam invenient
short: Jupiter declares strict neutrality: each side's own actions will bring its fortune; he is the same king to all; 'the fates will find their way'.
body: These lines are the core of Jupiter's ruling. 'Each man's undertakings shall bring him his toil and fortune' leaves the outcome to human choice; 'King Jupiter is the same to all' promises impartiality; 'the fates will find a way' (fata viam invenient) repeats Helenus' assurance at 3.395. Conington and Nettleship note that 'nec Rutulos solvo' (I do not release the Rutulians, 10.111) means Jupiter will not excuse the side that currently has the advantage. Scholars have long debated how Jupiter's will relates to fate in the Aeneid: elsewhere he speaks as the revealer of fate (1.257-96) and here as an umpire standing back from it. The neutrality does not last, since in 10.606-27 he allows Juno to rescue Turnus for a time, and in Book XII he weighs the two heroes' fates in his scales (12.725-7).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 246, note on 10.111 and 10.113
S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.111-13

title: The Etruscans as 'Lydians'
greek: libera fati / classem conscendit iussis gens Lydia divum / externo commissa duci
short: Virgil follows the tradition that the Etruscans came from Lydia in Asia Minor; an oracle had forbidden them any Italian leader, so they follow Aeneas.
body: 'Lydian' and 'Maeonian' are Virgil's regular names for the Etruscans. The tradition goes back to Herodotus (1.94), who says that during a famine half the Lydians sailed west under Tyrrhenus, son of their king, and settled among the Umbrians, taking the name Tyrrhenians. Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Roman Antiquities 1.30) argued instead that they were native to Italy, so the question was already debated in antiquity. In Book VIII the Etruscans, having expelled the tyrant Mezentius, were held back by a soothsayer's warning that no Italian could lead them: 'choose foreign leaders' (externos optate duces, 8.503). Now, 'freed from' that oracle (libera fati), they embark under the foreigner Aeneas. Conington and Nettleship cross-refer 'gens Lydia' to 8.479 and 'externo duci' to 8.503. The Lydian origin also gives the Etruscans an eastern kinship with the Trojans.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 250, note on 10.155-156

anchor: Open now the gates of Helicon
title: Invocation and catalogue of the Etruscan ships
greek: Pandite nunc Helicona, deae, cantusque movete
short: A fresh call to the Muses introduces a catalogue of Aeneas' Etruscan allies, ship by ship, answering the catalogue of Italians at the end of Book VII.
body: The line repeats the invocation that opened the catalogue of Latin forces (7.641); Helicon, the Boeotian mountain, is the Muses' home. Both catalogues imitate Homer's Catalogue of Ships, with its own appeal to the Muses (Iliad 2.484-93). Virgil's list is short and set at sea: each captain's ship is named after its figurehead or painted emblem (the Tiger, an Apollo, the Centaur, the Triton), as in the boat-race of Book V. Conington and Nettleship summarise the first part: Massicus with a thousand men from Clusium and Cosae; Abas with six hundred from Populonia and three hundred from Ilva (Elba, famous for its iron mines); the seer Asilas with a thousand from Pisa, a city said to have been founded from Pisa in Elis on the river Alpheus (hence 'of Alphaean birth'); Astyr with three hundred from Caere, Pyrgi and Graviscae. Then come the Ligurian Cinyras and Cupavo, Ocnus of Mantua and Aulestes, thirty ships in all.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 251, note on 10.163-184 and 10.163
S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.163-214

title: Asilas the seer and Etruscan divination
greek: hominum divumque interpres Asilas, / cui pecudum fibrae, caeli cui sidera parent / et linguae volucrum et praesagi fulminis ignes
short: Asilas commands every branch of Etruscan divination: entrails, stars, the speech of birds and the lightning that foretells.
body: The Etruscans were famous in Rome for their 'discipline' (Etrusca disciplina), the lore of reading the will of the gods. Asilas embodies it: he reads the entrails of victims (haruspicy), the stars, the cries and flight of birds (augury), and lightning. Cicero says that Etruria was especially skilled in interpreting things struck from the sky and in explaining what each portent meant (De divinatione 1.92). Conington and Nettleship point out that the phrase 'interpreter of the gods' is used of the seer Helenus (3.359, where a similar list follows), and that Cicero calls augurs the 'interpreters and messengers' of Jupiter (Philippics 13.5.12); adding 'of men' here brings out the root sense of interpres, a go-between who stands between two parties; Servius likewise calls the word 'medium', facing both ways, and cites Nigidius Figulus for the view that the arts of divination are so linked that one cannot be had without the others. Etruscan haruspices were still consulted by the Roman state in Virgil's day.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 252, note on 10.175
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.175
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. interpres

title: Cycnus and Phaethon
greek: namque ferunt luctu Cycnum Phaethontis amati, / populeas inter frondes umbramque sororum / dum canit
short: Cupavo wears swan's plumes because his father Cycnus, mourning his beloved Phaethon, was turned into a swan as he sang.
body: Phaethon, son of the Sun, lost control of his father's chariot and was struck down by Jupiter into the river Eridanus (the Po); his sisters, the Heliades, grieving, became poplars. Cycnus ('Swan'), a Ligurian king who loved him, sang his grief among those poplar 'sisters' and was changed into the bird, his white feathers figured as white old age ('canentem molli pluma duxisse senectam'). Ovid tells both stories at length in Metamorphoses 2.319-380. Conington and Nettleship note that the Phaethon legend had been located in Liguria (citing Polybius 2.16 and Ovid's 'Ligurum populos ... rexerat'); they also discuss 'crimen amor vestrum' (your love the reproach), which Mackail takes as an address to Love; it may instead mean 'the fault of your love', addressed to father and son. The swan feathers on Cupavo's crest are a 'blazon' (insigne) of his father's shape.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 253, note on 10.185, 10.189-190 and 10.192

title: Mantua and the Mincius (Virgil's homeland)
greek: qui muros matrisque dedit tibi, Mantua, nomen, / Mantua dives avis
short: Virgil, born near Mantua, salutes his own city in the catalogue, naming its legendary founder Ocnus and its river Mincius.
body: Ocnus, son of the prophetess Manto and the Tuscan river (the Tiber), founded Mantua and named it after his mother. Virgil's apostrophe ('who gave thee, O Mantua, ramparts and his mother's name') is a personal signature: his birthplace was Andes near Mantua, and he praised the green banks of the Mincius in Georgics 3.12-15 and Eclogue 7.12-13. The city is 'rich in ancestry' but of mixed race: three peoples, each divided into four communities, with the Etruscans dominant. Conington and Nettleship record a rival legend that derived the name from Mantus, an Etruscan name of the god of the dead. The five hundred Mantuans sail under a figurehead of the river Mincius, 'child of Benacus' because it flows out of Lake Benacus (Lago di Garda), crowned with grey reeds; Conington rejects the older idea that they were sailing down the Mincius itself.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 254, note on 10.200 and 10.205-206

title: Cymodocea and the ship-nymphs
greek: quarum quae fandi doctissima Cymodocea
short: Aeneas' former ships, turned into sea-nymphs by Cybele in Book IX, meet him at night and warn him that the camp is under siege.
body: In 9.77-122 Turnus tried to burn the Trojan fleet, built from pines of Mount Ida sacred to Cybele, and the goddess turned the ships into nymphs. Now they swim up in formation to Aeneas' flagship; Cymodocea, the most eloquent, explains who they are, tells him Ascanius is besieged and that Turnus means to block the Arcadian and Etruscan cavalry, and pushes the ship on with her hand. Her name is that of a Nereid (Georgics 4.338; Aeneid 5.826). Conington and Nettleship find 'fandi doctissima' (most skilled in speech) weak, and report Servius' scorn for those who explained it by saying she had been Ilioneus' ship (Ilioneus being the Trojan spokesman). The line is modelled on 1.72. The episode, which some critics thought too fantastic, links the Trojan fleet to the Great Mother, whom Aeneas at once invokes (10.252-5). Ovid retells the transformation in Metamorphoses 14.527-565.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 257, note on 10.225

title: Aeneas' helmet like a comet or Sirius
greek: non secus ac liquida si quando nocte cometae / sanguinei lugubre rubent, aut Sirius ardor
short: As Aeneas raises his divine shield, his helmet and shield-boss blaze like ominous comets or the Dog Star that brings drought and disease.
body: Virgil combines two Homeric pictures: the fire that Athena kindles on Diomedes' helmet and shield (Iliad 5.4-7), and Akhilleus, seen by Priam, shining like the star called Orion's Dog, which brings fever to wretched mortals (Iliad 22.25-32). Conington and Nettleship observe that the comets are Virgil's addition, unknown to Homer, and would recall to Roman readers the comets that terrified Rome in the civil wars, although the comet after Caesar's death in 44 BC was also hailed as a good sign. Servius explains that comets could portend good or ill depending on the planet they came from. The beauty of the hero is thus made frightening: for the Rutulians Aeneas' arrival is a portent of death. Milton imitated the image for Satan, who 'like a comet burn'd ... and from his horrid hair / Shakes pestilence and war' (Paradise Lost 2.708-11), as Conington notes.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 260, note on 10.272-273 and 10.275
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.272

title: 'Audentis Fortuna iuvat'
greek: audentis Fortuna iuvat
short: Turnus' rallying cry is a proverb, 'Fortune helps the bold'; it ends an unfinished half-line, and Turnus' daring will not in fact be rewarded.
body: Servius at once identifies the proverb and quotes Terence, 'fortis fortuna adiuvat' (Phormio 203); it was a commonplace, and Pliny the Younger reports that his uncle used it before sailing towards Vesuvius in AD 79 (Letters 6.16.11). Turnus urges his men to attack the Trojans at the water's edge while their footing is unsteady. The line is one of the unfinished half-lines (hemistichs) left in the poem at Virgil's death; Mackail marks the break with dots. Its placement is ironic: Turnus will be drawn away from the battle by Juno's phantom later in the book, and his boldness leads to his death in Book XII. Compare Turnus' last speeches, where he speaks of Fortune and the gods turning against him (12.676-80, 12.894-5).

sources.cite: Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.284

anchor: cut from his mother already dead
title: Lichas, born by caesarean section, sacred to Apollo
greek: inde Lichan ferit exsectum iam matre perempta / et tibi, Phoebe, sacrum
short: Lichas, cut from his dead mother's womb, was consecrated to Apollo, god of healing; his 'escape' from the knife at birth makes his death by the sword pathetic.
body: Servius (on 10.316), quoted by Conington and Nettleship, explains that all who are born by cutting the womb were consecrated to Apollo, because he is the god of medicine through whose art they came into the light; this, he says, is why Aesculapius, Apollo's son, was imagined as born in that way. Servius also linked the worship of Apollo in the Julian family to a story that the first Caesar was so born; Conington calls the story 'exploded'. Pliny the Elder records the belief that the first of the Caesars got his name 'a caeso matris utero' (Natural History 7.47). The point in the narrative is pathos: the child who once escaped 'the perilous steel' falls to Aeneas' sword. Such brief biographies of victims are a Homeric technique (for example Iliad 5.59-68 on Phereclus) that Virgil uses constantly in the battle books.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 265, note on 10.315
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.316

anchor: the Fates laid hand on him
title: 'Iniecere manum Parcae': the Fates make an arrest
greek: iniecere manum Parcae telisque sacrarunt / Evandri
short: Virgil describes Halesus' doom in legal language: the Fates 'laid hands on' him, as a Roman creditor seized a debtor, and consecrated him to Evander's weapons.
body: Halesus' father, a seer, had hidden him in the woods to escape death, but when the old man died 'the Fates laid hand on him'. Servius explains that Virgil is using the language of law: manus iniectio is the act by which, without waiting for a judge's authority, we seize what is owed to us. Conington and Nettleship add that the phrases manum inicere and manus iniectio, for hauling a man into court, are as old as the Twelve Tables. The metaphor makes death a debt that must be paid. Servius also comments on 'sacrarunt' (consecrated): whatever is destined for the gods is called sacer, and the soul can reach the gods only when freed from the body. Pallas kills Halesus a few lines later (10.424-5).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 274, note on 10.419
Servius, In Vergilii Aeneidos commentarii (ed. G. Thilo, Leipzig 1881), note on Aen. 10.419
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. inicio (injicio), manum inicere

anchor: thine oak shall bear these arms
title: Pallas' vow: the spoils hung on an oak
greek: da nunc, Thybri pater, ferro, quod missile libro, / fortunam atque viam duri per pectus Halaesi. / haec arma exuviasque viri tua quercus habebit
short: Pallas promises Father Tiber the armour of Halesus, to be hung on an oak: the old Roman custom of the trophy.
body: Before throwing, Pallas makes a conditional vow (votum) in proper Roman form: give my weapon a way through Halesus' breast, and his arms and clothing will hang on 'your oak'. Conington and Nettleship discuss whether this means an oak already sacred to the river-god (as the wild olive sacred to Faunus in 12.766) or one that will be consecrated to him, preferring the second; they compare Livy 1.10, where Romulus hangs the spoils of King Acron on an oak sacred to shepherds before dedicating the first spolia opima to Jupiter Feretrius. The Tiber is Pallas' natural patron, since the river god had appeared to Aeneas and sent him to Evander's city (8.31-78). The vow is granted; Aeneas will build exactly such a trophy from Mezentius' armour at the opening of Book XI.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 275, note on 10.423

title: Hercules weeps; 'stat sua cuique dies'
greek: magnumque sub imo / corde premit gemitum lacrimasque effundit inanis ... stat sua cuique dies, breve et inreparabile tempus / omnibus est vitae; sed famam extendere factis, / hoc virtutis opus
short: Pallas prays to Hercules, his father's guest; Hercules can only weep, and Jupiter consoles him: every man has his fixed day, but fame is won by deeds.
body: Pallas appeals to Hercules by 'my father's hospitality and the board whereto thou camest a wanderer': Evander had entertained Hercules after he killed Cacus (8.185-305). Hercules, himself once a mortal hero, stifles a groan and sheds useless tears. Conington and Nettleship note that the scene comes from Iliad 16.431-61, where Zeus weeps tears of blood for his son Sarpedon, whom he will not save; Jupiter here even cites Sarpedon ('mine own child Sarpedon likewise perished'). Jupiter's consolation is among the most quoted lines of the poem: 'each has his own appointed day; short and irrecoverable is the span of life for all; but to extend fame by deeds, that is the work of valour'. Conington compares 'hoc opus, hic labor est' (6.129). Jupiter adds that Turnus too has reached the end of his allotted time, and turns his eyes from the field.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 278, note on 10.464-465, 10.469 and 10.470

title: 'Qualem meruit': Turnus returns Pallas' body
greek: Arcades, haec ... Evandro: qualem meruit, Pallanta remitto
short: Turnus sends Pallas back to Evander 'as he deserved', mocking the old king for his alliance with Aeneas, but grants burial.
body: Standing over Pallas, Turnus tells the Arcadians to carry his words to Evander: 'I send him back his Pallas as he deserved (to see him)'. Conington and Nettleship take the phrase as a taunt, 'such as he deserved to see him after his alliance with Aeneas', and reject Heyne's milder sense, 'dead but honourably dead', which mistakes Turnus' feeling. Turnus then grants 'whatever honour there is in a tomb, whatever comfort in burial', which is the minimum heroic custom requires, but adds that Evander will pay dearly for his hospitality to Aeneas. The speech, followed at once by the stripping of the sword-belt with his foot on the corpse, sets up the reader's judgement of Turnus at the end of the poem. Contrast Aeneas, who returns Lausus' body and arms untouched (10.825-32).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 280, note on 10.492
S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.491-500

title: The sword-belt of Pallas (the Danaids)
greek: immania pondera baltei / impressumque nefas: una sub nocte iugali / caesa manus iuvenum foede thalamique cruenti
short: Turnus strips from Pallas a heavy gold belt engraved with the Danaids' murder of their bridegrooms; the same belt will cost him his life in the poem's last scene.
body: The baldric (balteus) shows the story of the fifty daughters of Danaus, who on their wedding night killed their fifty cousin-husbands, the sons of Aegyptus; only Hypermestra spared hers (Apollodorus, Library 2.1.5). Conington and Nettleship explain 'impressum nefas' as the scene of horror stamped upon the metal, made in gold by the otherwise unknown Clonus son of Eurytus. Critics have seen the subject as apt to Pallas: young men killed before their marriage could be fulfilled, a 'crime' that calls for vengeance. Augustus' new temple of Apollo on the Palatine (dedicated 28 BC) had a portico with statues of the Danaids (Propertius 2.31.3-4), so the image would also have been familiar to Virgil's readers. Turnus wears the belt as a trophy; in 12.941-9 the sight of it on his shoulder ends Aeneas' hesitation, as the narrator immediately warns (10.501-5).

S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.495-505

title: 'Nescia mens hominum': the narrator's warning
greek: nescia mens hominum fati sortisque futurae / et servare modum rebus sublata secundis!
short: The poet breaks in to lament human blindness and excess in success: Turnus will one day wish he had never touched Pallas or his spoils.
body: A rare direct comment from the narrator. Human minds are 'ignorant of fate and future lot, and of keeping measure (modum) when lifted up by success'; the time will come when Turnus would pay a great price to have left Pallas untouched, and will hate 'those spoils and that day'. The idea of measure and the danger of prosperity is a commonplace of Greek and Roman moral thought. The nearest Homeric model is Iliad 17.194-208, where Hector puts on Akhilleus' armour stripped from Patroclus and Zeus, pitying him, observes that he does not know how near death is. The prophecy is fulfilled to the letter in the last lines of the poem (12.938-52), so that the whole second half of Book XII is read in its light.

sources.cite: S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.501-5

title: Captives taken for sacrifice at Pallas' pyre
greek: Sulmone creatos / quattuor hic iuvenes, totidem quos educat Ufens, / viventis rapit, inferias quos immolet umbris / captivoque rogi perfundat sanguine flammas
short: In his grief Aeneas takes eight young men alive to be killed as offerings (inferiae) at Pallas' funeral, as Akhilleus did for Patroclus.
body: The model is Iliad 21.26-32, where Akhilleus takes twelve Trojan youths alive from the river as blood-price for Patroclus, and 23.175-6, where he kills them at the pyre. Inferiae are offerings to the dead; the captives reappear, hands bound, in the funeral procession of 11.81-2. Conington and Nettleship remark that in imitating Homer Virgil imputes to Aeneas a barbarity 'regarded with horror in his own day', and compare Livy's outrage (7.15) at the Tarquinians' sacrifice of Roman prisoners. The episode is one of the most disputed in the poem: some readers see a deliberate darkening of Aeneas, whose grief turns to fury; others see epic convention. Suetonius reports a hostile story that after the siege of Perusia in 40 BC Octavian had three hundred prisoners sacrificed at an altar of the deified Julius (Augustus 15), which some modern critics bring into the discussion.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 282, note on 10.518 and 10.519-520

title: Magus the suppliant
greek: et genua amplectens effatur talia supplex: / 'per patrios Manis et spes surgentis Iuli ...'
short: Magus clasps Aeneas' knees and offers ransom, appealing to Anchises and Iulus; Aeneas refuses, saying Turnus ended all 'trading in war' when he killed Pallas.
body: Clasping the knees is the ritual gesture of supplication, which puts the suppliant under the protection of the gods. Magus follows the Homeric pattern exactly: he appeals to what the victor holds dearest and offers gold and silver as ransom, like Adrestus to Menelaus (Iliad 6.45-65) or Lycaon to Akhilleus (Iliad 21.64-119). Aeneas' answer turns the appeal back: it is precisely the ghost of Anchises and Iulus who demand his death, and 'belli commercia', the trade of ransom in war, ended when Pallas fell. Conington and Nettleship note that Aeneas undertakes to interpret Anchises' and Iulus' wishes himself, and compare Pyrrhus killing Priam, gripping his hair, in 2.552-3. Aeneas' rejection of a suppliant here is the first of a series that leads to the final rejection of Turnus' plea in 12.930-52.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 284, note on 10.534-535

title: Aeneas' taunt over Tarquitus: denial of burial
greek: istic nunc, metuende, iace. non te optima mater / condet humi patrioque onerabit membra sepulcro
short: Aeneas tells the dying Tarquitus that no mother will bury him; birds or fish will have his body, the worst fate a warrior could be threatened with.
body: Burial was a sacred duty; to be left unburied meant shame for the dead and, in Roman belief, a restless shade (compare Palinurus, 6.325-83). Conington and Nettleship identify the double Homeric model: Odysseus over Socus, whose father and mother will not close his eyes but birds will tear him (Iliad 11.452-5), and Akhilleus over Lycaon, whose body the river fish will lick (Iliad 21.122-7). The sarcastic 'metuende' (formidable one) mocks Tarquitus' 'pride of glittering arms'. These words are among the harshest Aeneas speaks; together with the human sacrifice and the killing of Magus they show his fury after Pallas' death. Burial becomes a dominant theme of the last books: Mezentius begs for it (10.903-6), the truce of Book XI is made to bury the dead, and Turnus asks for his body to be returned (12.935-6).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 286, note on 10.557

title: Aeneas compared to Aegaeon (Briareus)
greek: Aegaeon qualis, centum cui bracchia dicunt / centenasque manus ... Iovis cum fulmina contra / tot paribus streperet clipeis
short: Raging over the field, Aeneas is likened to the hundred-handed giant who fought against Jupiter's thunderbolts.
body: Aegaeon is the giant also called Briareus, one of the Hundred-Handers ('centumgeminus Briareus', 6.287). In Homer he is Zeus' ally, summoned by Thetis to protect him from a rebellion of the other gods (Iliad 1.401-6), and in Hesiod the Hundred-Handers fight for Zeus against the Titans (Theogony 147-53, 617-735). Virgil chooses a version in which Aegaeon fights against Jupiter, with fifty mouths breathing fire and fifty shields clashing against the thunderbolts. Conington and Nettleship note the Homeric contrast. Comparing the pious hero to a monster in revolt against the supreme god is startling, and critics disagree about how much to make of it: some read it as a sign that Aeneas' rage has made him, for the moment, an enemy of the order he serves; others see a simple image of multiplied strength. Compare the gigantomachy imagery used of Turnus and of the shield of Aeneas.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 287, note on 10.565
S. J. Harrison, Vergil: Aeneid 10 (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1991), notes on 10.565-70

title: Juno's phantom of Aeneas
greek: tum dea nube cava tenuem sine viribus umbram / in faciem Aeneae (visu mirabile monstrum) / Dardaniis ornat telis
short: With Jupiter's leave, Juno makes a phantom of Aeneas from hollow cloud; Turnus chases it onto a ship and is carried away from the battle.
body: Jupiter has allowed Juno only delay, not rescue (10.622-7). She shapes an image (an eidolon) of Aeneas out of 'hollow cloud', with his arms, voice and gait. Conington and Nettleship identify the model as Iliad 5.449-53, where Apollo, having carried Aeneas out of the fight, makes a phantom like him for the Greeks and Trojans to fight over; Virgil reverses the situation, so that the image of Aeneas is used to save his enemy. Turnus' cry 'forsake not thy plighted bridal chamber' is ironic, since Lavinia is the prize of the war. Carried out to sea, Turnus does not feel rescued but disgraced: he asks the winds to wreck him and three times thinks of suicide, while Juno holds him back. The episode keeps Turnus alive for Book XII and shows how much his sense of honour (pudor) governs him.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 293, note on 10.636

title: 'Dextra mihi deus': Mezentius' prayer to his own hand
greek: dextra mihi deus et telum, quod missile libro, / nunc adsint!
short: Mezentius, 'despiser of the gods', prays only to his own right hand and spear, and vows Lausus as a living trophy dressed in Aeneas' spoils.
body: Mezentius was introduced as 'contemptor divum' (7.648), and here his godlessness takes the form of a parody of prayer: his right hand is his god. Conington and Nettleship cite the closest Greek models: Parthenopaeus in Aeschylus' Seven against Thebes (529-32), who swears by his spear and honours it above a god, and Idas in Apollonius' Argonautica (1.466-8), who boasts that his spear helps him more than Zeus. He vows to make Lausus himself the trophy (tropaeum), dressed in the armour stripped from 'the pirate' Aeneas. The vow fails at once: the spear glances off and kills Antores, and Lausus dies defending his father. Mezentius' later address to his horse Rhaebus, and his recognition of guilt (10.846-56), give this hard figure an unexpected depth.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 305, note on 10.773

title: The death of Lausus: the poet's apostrophe
greek: hic mortis durae casum tuaque optima facta, / si qua fidem tanto est operi latura vetustas, / non equidem nec te, iuvenis memorande, silebo
short: Before Lausus dies saving his father, the poet turns to address him, promising that his deed will not go unsung.
body: Lausus, Mezentius' son, steps in when his wounded father withdraws, and holds off Aeneas while Mezentius escapes. The narrator interrupts with a direct address, a device Virgil uses for the dead he most honours, as for Nisus and Euryalus ('fortunati ambo', 9.446-9). Conington and Nettleship discuss the reading 'optima' and compare Cicero's phrase 'mortis casus' (On Old Age 19). The clause 'if antiquity will win belief for so great a deed' admits that such loyalty might seem incredible. Lausus' devotion to a bad father mirrors Aeneas' own pietas towards Anchises, which is why Aeneas, after killing him, is overwhelmed by the 'image of filial love'. Lausus had been introduced in the catalogue of Book VII as worthy of a better father (7.649-54).

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 306, note on 10.791

title: 'Patriae pietatis imago': Aeneas over Lausus
greek: ingemuit miserans graviter dextramque tetendit, / et mentem patriae subiit pietatis imago. / 'quid tibi nunc, miserande puer, pro laudibus istis, / quid pius Aeneas tanta dabit indole dignum?'
short: Seeing the dying boy's face, Aeneas thinks of his own love for his father, calls himself 'pius', and gives Lausus back to his people with his armour.
body: The phrase 'patriae pietatis imago' is ambiguous: the picture of devotion to a father, Lausus' and also Aeneas' own towards Anchises. Conington and Nettleship note that the line nearly repeats 9.294, where Ascanius is moved by Euryalus' love for his mother, and they call 'pius' in 10.826 emphatic: Aeneas names himself by his defining virtue at the moment he has killed a son devoted to his father. Pietas in Latin means dutiful love towards gods, country and family. Aeneas refuses to strip the body, the opposite of Turnus' treatment of Pallas, and offers the consolation that Lausus fell by 'great Aeneas' hand', a heroic commonplace (compare Camilla to Ornytus, 11.688-9). He lifts the body himself, its hair stained with blood. The scene is often read as the moral counterweight to the killing of Turnus.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 309, note on 10.824 and 10.826
C. T. Lewis and C. Short, A Latin Dictionary (Oxford, 1879), s.v. pietas

title: Mezentius' last request: burial with his son
greek: corpus humo patiare tegi. scio acerba meorum / circumstare odia: hunc, oro, defende furorem / et me consortem nati concede sepulcro
short: The defeated Mezentius asks no mercy, only that Aeneas protect his body from his people's hatred and bury him with Lausus; then he takes the sword.
body: Mezentius' final speech refuses to beg for life ('naught forbids my slaughter'), which separates him from the suppliants Aeneas has killed. His one request is burial, and he gives the reason: his own Etruscan subjects hate him for his cruelty (8.481-95) and would abuse his corpse. Conington and Nettleship quote the late commentator Tiberius Donatus: he feared his people, mindful of an old and just hatred, would tear his body apart and do to the dead what they could not do to the living. They also explain 'haud inscius accipit ensem' (he receives the sword knowingly): the phrase recalls 'ferrum recipere', used of a defeated gladiator who offers himself to the death-stroke (compare Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 2.41). The book ends abruptly with his death; Virgil does not say whether the request was granted. Compare Turnus' plea in 12.930-8.

sources.cite: J. Conington and H. Nettleship, P. Vergili Maronis Opera, vol. 3: The Last Six Books of the Aeneid (3rd ed., London: Whittaker and Bell, 1883), p. 316, note on 10.903, 10.904-905 and 10.907
